Intermittent fasting - The second step on the road to health

This is the second part of this series. You can find the first part, and a short introduction of me here.

You've probably heard that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. But actually it is the other way around that is true - Breakfast is the most important meal of the day to avoid. This is why:

When we eat, the immune system is put to work, killing all the bacteria and neutralizing toxins that accompany food. Sometimes the amounts of bad stuff are higher than the nutritional value, and our senses of smell and taste does the job of preventing us from eating things that are for example rotten or foul. Sadly we are today exposed to things called food that should never be called that. The evolution have not prepared us for processed carbohydrates and vegetable oils (see my previous post). If it had, we would probably vomit instead of thinking they smell and taste delicious, because those kind of "foods" are without question more damaging than their nutritional value justifies. But even perfectly fresh, natural and nutritional food contains some amount of toxic stuff that must be dealt with. And the process of converting the food to nutrients is also hard work for our body. Because of this, other processes like repairing cell damage, producing new cells and hormones, are put on hold while digestion takes place. So as you can see, while eating is of course necessary, the activity in itself comes with a high cost.

Therefor it's reasonable to have a low frequency eating pattern and to eat food with a high calorie content that keeps you satiated longer. Some scientists thinks sleeping is a mystery, but to me it's self evident that sleeping occurs because the body requires undisturbed maintenance time. During sleep it's certain that no harmful eating occurs and the body can focus on other things that need to be taken care of. But we can actually prolong this healthy maintenance window by, as you probably guessed, skipping breakfast.

Ancel Keys was a famous nutritional researcher in the 60s that got some things right, but sadly most of them wrong. Keys studied the Mediterranean countries because people were healthier and lived longer there, compared to the rest of the world. And he concluded it was because of a diet that contains more olive oil, fish, whole grains and vegetables. And he may have been right about that. But then he got it wrong by claiming that it was the unsaturated aspect of those fats that made them healthier. Another key thing that Keys (oops pun!) failed to notice about the Mediterranean is that breakfast is usually no more than a cup of coffee or a glass of water.

So there you have it dear ketoers - skip breakfast and don't eat to often, and when you do, make sure you stuff yourself with lots of healthy calorie rich fats! Or with a more "professional" vocabulary - Take up 16:8 intermittent fasting and eat keto so you'll stay full.

To me it's a blessing to not have to mess with breakfast during the stressful weekdays and I can tell my body thanks me for it. I keep a bottle of cream at work and usually just have a cup of coffee with cream and a glass of water in the morning ours. On weekends however, I eat gourmet breakfasts with my family. Another benefit that I contribute partly to intermittent fasting is that I require less sleep. Since I eat fewer times and also better food, less nightly maintenance is required and I typically wake up 1-2 hours earlier.

This was the second part of my write ups for /v/keto. The first parts covered the "donts" - Don't eat processed food and don't eat breakfast. The following parts will be "dos". Stay tuned for the third part: Eat butter - The third step on the road to health

Just got my CCW a few weeks ago. Anybody here have some advice for a newbie?

What training have you had? Safe gun handling, safe storage, and a full knowledge of the applicable laws are very important now.

What state are you in? The laws vary a lot, and if there is a chance you might cross a state or city line with your CCW, that can matter too.

Have you selected a firearm yet? Have you given thought to how you'd like to carry it, and how that will be influenced by how you dress? Do you have a job that will cause trouble for you if you are found to be carrying?

How well do you shoot? How often do you practice?

I am in Virginia, so I know Maryland is a no no. I received gun training from an FBI agent who is a friend of the family. As for how I plan on carrying it, I'm flexible and currently experimenting with what way works best for me.

If you are confident that you have the gun basics down pat, the next item on the list is to learn about the law. The law is tricky, counterintuitive, often illogical or unfair, and you can get into very expensive trouble if you get tangled in it.

I don't know your particular state so I'll just mention some of the things I've known that have come up. Some probably apply to you.

First, if open carry is disallowed, you might get into trouble if your gun 'prints' and becomes unintentionally visible to another person. This is not technically illegal but it can ruin your day. Be aware that intentionally displaying your gun to another person - 'brandishing' - is usually a felony. Some folks will do this to forestall a potential threat, not realizing that they have committed a serious crime. Some states require you to mention that you have your gun when you get pulled over for a speeding ticket. Some states require you to retreat from a public space before fighting, others allow you to hold your ground in public. In many places, a well-intentioned warning shot may be taken as a tacit admission that your life was not in imminent danger. It can also be take as justification for the other person to decide that you, not they, had escalated the fight to a deadly level and allowed them to resort to deadly force in response.

Knowing what to say (very little) and what not to say (everything else) to the police after a shooting is no less a lifesaving skill than shooting quickly and well. The judicial system can sometimes cause you more harm than your attacker will.

So I'd strongly suggest a good CCW class in your area to learn how much of this stuff applies to you.

Beyond that, my general advice is that getting involved in a fight, even if you were fully justified, always means an expensive and dangerous tangle with the law. Even a bullshit little shoving match becomes a big problem if you are armed and need to protect your gun. Avoid trouble twice as much as you normally would. Walk away, stay away, run away if it will work.

Consider how you will handle your gun in a public toilet (do NOT remove it from your control and leave it behind)! Consider how you will sit with it in a car seat, how you can reach it in your car seat, how you can store it in your car when entering a gun free zone. Don't wear it across your spine, you can suffer a nasty injury if you get knocked down. The smallest, flattest, lightest gun that you can still shoot well is the one you want.

If pulled over by an officer hand over you license and your CCW permit. This way he knows you are not trying to hide anything. Also, if I am not mistaken, some states require you to do so.

Familiarize yourself with your state laws regarding carrying a weapon. What places are ok and which ones are off limits.

Familiarize yourself with the states that reciprocate for your permit. Follow all the CCW laws of the reciprocating state when in that state.

EDIT: www.usacarry.com and handgunlaws.us are pretty good resources.
I really appreciate the links, I'll check them out right away.

Get in the habit of always carrying where legal. Don't say to yourself I'm just going to pick up the dry cleaning and won't need my weapon. You may very well. You never know so always carry. Just saying...

Practice drawing and re- holstering in addition to shooting. If you have a Glock or other piece that doesn't have a safety, take special care on the re-holstering as an AD (glock leg) can occur if the trigger is depressed accidentally.

Carrying is a special responsibility. Be smart but don't hesitate to protect yourself and your family. And if you have kids, be very careful with your weapon but also teach them about the pistol so they know it's a deadly tool and not a toy. Gun lock or gun safe! Most states have laws requiring such if kids might have access.

Steer clear of crappy holsters they can bunch up in your trigger guard.

What are you carrying?
Right now, just a Tanfoglio 380. Not the best gun in the world, but it's a hand-me-down and I can't afford anything else right now.

Don't touch your gun every few minutes if you can help it. it makes you more suspicious than a little printing here and there and people aren't that observant, anyway.

Fairly straightforward, but I've heard of people carrying with their cheap FMJ range ammo. Don't do this! Not only is it less effective for the intended purpose, but the point that hit home for me was that you want it to penetrate as little beyond your target as possible. You're already going to be in a legal mess if you have to use it.

Find and consult with a lawyer before you start carrying. Seriously. Match the dollars that you spend on your pistol and holster with dollars spent with an attorney who has solid experience in self-defense and the law in your jurisdiction. Some states require CCW classes to include instruction from an attorney. More than a decade ago I was advised that even a completely clean and righteous shooting will likely cost you upwards of $100,000 and at least a few friendships. The choice to draw your gun can end the other person's life and ruin yours. Do your homework ahead of time and be absolutely sure that the alternative is worse.
